title: Measuring correlations in quantum and statistical systems
authors: V. I. Yukalov, E. P. Yukalova
abstract: The survey discusses the problem of measuring correlations in composite quantum and statistical systems. After briefly recalling the standard methods of describing correlations, the emphasis is on the method of correlation indices. The latter method for quantifying the strength of correlations in composite physical systems is sufficiently general allowing for measuring in a unique way the correlation strength in both quantum and statistical systems, for static as well as for dynamic processes. The correlation indices, can be defined for correlation operators, reduced density matrices, and other operators containing information on correlations in the studied composite systems. The correlation indices measure all types of correlations, quantum correlations, such as entanglement, as well as classical correlations. They are applicable for characterizing static as well as dynamical processes. Examples are given of correlation indices for several quantum states and for spin and pseudospin systems. The quantification of correlations in a nonequilibrium system is exemplified by calculating the correlation index for a trapped Bose-Einstein condensate subject to the action of an alternating field.
summary: This theoretical survey introduces the correlation index ($\kappa$) as a universal diagnostic tool to quantify correlation strength in quantum and statistical systems. By comparing correlation operators to their factorized counterparts, $\kappa$ measures both quantum entanglement and classical correlations. It is demonstrated through applications to spin systems and time-dependent BEC dynamics, providing a powerful quantitative measure for many-body physics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the general problem of quantitatively measuring the strength of correlations—both classical and quantum—within composite quantum and statistical systems.
main_result: The introduction of a 'correlation index' ($\kappa$) provides a general, quantitative measure applicable across various physical regimes, successfully quantifying both entanglement and classical correlations.
method: The core method involves defining a correlation index, $\kappa(\hat{C}) \equiv \ln  rac{||\hat{C}||}{||\hat{C}^{\otimes}||}$, which compares the norm of a correlation operator ($\hat{C}$) to its factorized, uncorrelated counterpart ($\hat{C}^{\otimes}$).
model_or_system: The method is applied to diverse systems, including spin systems, general N-partite quantum states, and specifically, a trapped Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) in a double-well potential subjected to an alternating field.
key_observables: Correlation index ($\kappa$), entanglement entropy ($S$), reduced density matrices ($\hat{ho}_A$), and correlation operators ($\hat{C}_n$).
important_parameters: Pumping parameter ($b$), system size ($N$), and the nature of the correlation (classical vs. quantum).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the existence of a general correlation operator $\hat{C}_n$ and its factorized counterpart $\hat{C}^{\otimes}_n$. For spin systems, the mean-field approximation is used.
figures_summary: The figures illustrate the time evolution of the correlation index ($\kappa(\hat{ho})$) for the BEC system under different pumping field amplitudes ($b$), showing maxima at $z=0$ and minima at $z=\pm 1$.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the general concept of correlation indices, then applies it to specific quantum states (EPR, Bell states) and spin systems, culminating in a detailed, time-dependent analysis of a BEC in a double-well potential.
why_interesting: The development of a single, unified metric ($\kappa$) to quantify all types of correlations (quantum entanglement and classical statistical correlations) is highly valuable for analyzing complex, non-equilibrium many-body dynamics in AMO physics.
